title: Microsoft's Python Agent Framework Hijacked to Spread Malware, AI Uncovers Critical NGINX Flaws, and Nadella Explains 60,000 AI-Era Buyouts
subhead: Attackers compromise Microsoft's official Python agent framework on GitHub to distribute malware as AI tools uncover critical bugs in NGINX across 225 million websites, Satya Nadella warns critical infrastructure is 'unpatchable,' and Anthropic prices its IPO at $1.5 trillion.

sections.heading: Microsoft's Python Agent Framework Hijacked to Distribute Malware
sections.body:
Attackers compromised GitHub organization admin credentials to hijack Microsoft's official Python AI agent framework and distribute malware to developers, The Register reports, compounding a difficult week for the software giant following recent Outlook disruptions. In a separate warning at the DealBook Summit, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella told audiences that much of the world's critical infrastructure is effectively 'unpatchable,' TechCrunch reports, even as AI tools expand both defensive auditing and automated attack surfaces.

Nadella also addressed Microsoft's October offer of voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees, explaining that the move aimed to reshape the workforce for AI-driven workflows rather than execute traditional mass layoffs, TechCrunch writes, while predicting that AI agents will disrupt ad-supported web economics and force giants like Amazon to rethink customer acquisition.
sections.whyItMatters: Compromising an official Microsoft AI agent repository turns developer trust into a direct supply-chain malware vector at the exact moment enterprises are rushing agentic frameworks into production.

sections.heading: AI Discovers Critical Bugs in NGINX Running 225M Websites
sections.body:
Automated AI vulnerability discovery uncovered critical security flaws in the open-source NGINX web server software powering roughly 225 million websites worldwide, The Register reports, adding to a wave of urgent enterprise patching following this week's Oracle Java alert. Separately, The Register warns that a critical PHP security release targeting at least one dangerous remote code execution (RCE) bug is scheduled to drop on Thursday.

Enterprise infrastructure teams also got a glimpse of Microsoft's security-first shift: Ars Technica reports the Windows Server 2028 public preview hardens default settings to align with Department of Defense standards, intentionally trading backward compatibility for tighter out-of-the-box protection.
sections.whyItMatters: AI-assisted bug hunting is finding high-severity flaws in foundational web infrastructure like NGINX and Java faster than many organizations can test and deploy patches.

sections.heading: Anthropic Prices $1.5T IPO as Musk Defends Huang and Backs Nvidia
sections.body:
Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share—above its expected range—implying a $1.5 trillion fully diluted valuation on the eve of its market debut, TechCrunch and Le Monde report, scheduling its listing on the same day as the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, The Register notes. Meanwhile, The Register reports MongoDB acquired Firebolt to unify analytical and transactional database workloads under one platform.

At Nvidia, fallout from former CEO Jensen Huang's ouster continued to ripple through Silicon Valley: TechCrunch reports Elon Musk compared removing Huang to 'kicking Michael Jordan off your team,' while Business Insider writes Nvidia is raising compensation to stop top engineers from leaving. Simultaneously, The Register cites Tencent warning that new US GPU bans set everyone back in China—while inevitably spurring domestic Chinese chipmakers to accelerate alternatives.
sections.whyItMatters: Anthropic's $1.5 trillion valuation confirms intense public demand for frontier AI equity, even as Nvidia's talent-retention battle and US GPU curbs accelerate semiconductor decoupling.

sections.heading: Meta Staffers Alarmed by Muse Privacy Flaws; Arizona Probes OpenAI
sections.body:
Internal chats reviewed by Ars Technica show Meta employees alarmed by erratic outputs from the company's Muse AI system appearing to share random bank and bitcoin balances—though Meta says the exposed figures are hallucinated rather than real user data. In parallel, CNA reports Arizona's attorney general opened an investigation into OpenAI and other AI developers over potential rogue agent incidents, following California's lawsuit earlier this week.

In US tech policy, Ars Technica reports a Ted Cruz-led Senate committee approved Trump's FCC nominee 15-0 amid a Democratic boycott, while the CFTC ordered prediction market Kalshi to halt contracts wagering on which specific words President Trump will say in speeches.
sections.whyItMatters: State-level investigations in Arizona and California alongside internal privacy scares at Meta show that unverified AI agent behavior is quickly turning into direct legal and regulatory liability.

sections.heading: Ukraine Uses Relay Drones to Bypass Starlink Limits; Korea Cuts Exam Wi-Fi
sections.body:
Battlefield connectivity took a pragmatic turn as Ars Technica reports Ukraine used homegrown aerial relay drones to bypass SpaceX Starshield speed limits over occupied territory during its latest strike on the Kerch Bridge, while Elon Musk accused President Zelenskyy of misusing consumer Starlink services for military strikes, The Verge writes. In South Korea, CNA and the New York Times report authorities cut Wi-Fi and issued nationwide phone alerts to combat AI-aided cheating during Thursday's high-stakes college entrance exam.

Elsewhere in consumer and automotive tech, Business Insider reports Tesla plans to build a steering-wheel-free autonomous Model Y alongside the Cybercab to carry more robotaxi passengers, while The Register notes Waymo suspended US freeway operations following construction-zone and patrol-car mishaps in California.
sections.whyItMatters: From relay drones overriding satellite restrictions to nationwide Wi-Fi blackouts during exams, operators are increasingly forced to build low-tech workarounds and hard guardrails around connected AI systems.

bottomLine: Software supply-chain security is emerging as the weak link of the AI boom: hijacked Microsoft Python agent packages and AI-discovered NGINX flaws threaten core infrastructure just as Anthropic prices a $1.5 trillion IPO. With state attorneys general probing rogue agents and US-China chip bans tightening, governance and security execution—not model capability alone—now define competitive risk.
sources: The Register, TechCrunch, Ars Technica, Le Monde, Business Insider, CNA, The Verge, New York Times
